Accessibility of Targets From Each Cell

Source: R/dp-accessibility.R
dp_accessibility.Rd

Usage

dp_accessibility(
  resistance,
  radius,
  source_strength = NULL,
  destination = NULL,
  site_radius = 2,
  source_threshold = 0.01,
  radius_units = c("pixels", "km"),
  resistance_is = "resistances",
  reference_resistance = 1,
  normalize = TRUE,
  n_draws = 64,
  seed = NULL,
  se = FALSE,
  contact = FALSE,
  progress = TRUE
)

Arguments

resistance

A terra::SpatRaster or file path: the resistance (or conductance) surface. Or a circuit from dp_circuit(), to reuse its factorization.

radius

Numeric. The dispersal radius: pairs of cells are counted if their centres are at most this far apart. In pixels by default (see radius_units). Inf counts all pairs.

source_strength

Optional terra::SpatRaster or file path on the same grid: target strength, e.g. habitat suitability. If NULL (default), the conductance surface is used, as in dp_omni(). With a destination, this is the origin strength: the targets of the destination_ layers.

destination

Optional terra::SpatRaster or file path on the same grid: destination strength, the targets of the origin_ layers. Default NULL: one set of targets.

site_radius

Number. The radius of the site each cell stands for (see "Sites"), in pixels, whatever radius_units. 0 is the cell alone. Default 2.

source_threshold

Numeric. Cells with source (or destination) strength below this are not sources (or destinations). Default 0.01.

radius_units

Character. "pixels" (default): the radius counts cells, so the kernel is the cells with \(dr^2 + dc^2 \le\) radius\(^2\), as in os_run(). "km": great-circle distance between cell centres on lon/lat grids (the kernel narrows in degrees of longitude towards the poles), or distance in the coordinate reference system's units, converted to km, on projected grids.

resistance_is

Character. Whether resistance holds "resistances" (default) or "conductances". Ignored for a circuit.

reference_resistance

Positive number. The resistance of the continuous habitat that accessible_area compares with, in the units of the input's resistance (also when resistance_is = "conductances"). Default 1.

normalize

Logical. Also return normalized_conductance (see "Method"). Default TRUE.

n_draws

Integer. Number of draws (solves). Default 64.

seed

Integer or NULL. Seed for the random draws. If NULL (default), one is drawn from R's random number generator, so set.seed() also makes runs reproducible. The seed used is returned as the "seed" attribute.

se

Logical. Also return each estimated layer's per-cell standard error, as layers with an _se suffix. Default FALSE.

contact

Logical. Also return each cell's contact conductance, the conductance of its own links in parallel, as the contact layer (see "Sites"). Default FALSE.

progress

Logical. Report progress through the 'progressr' package (see "Progress" in dp_omni()). Default TRUE; it shows only when a 'progressr' handler is active.

Value

A terra::SpatRaster with layers accessible_area (unless radius is Inf), target_area and conductance; with normalize, normalized_conductance; and with se, an _se layer for each but target_area, which is exact. With a destination, this set of layers twice, prefixed origin_ and destination_. With contact, a last layer contact. Cells off the circuit are NA, as is normalized_conductance where a cell has no targets. Attributes: "area_units" ("km2" or "cells"), "relative_se" (each estimated layer's median relative standard error over the cells with targets) and "seed".

Details

Maps how much of its targets each cell can reach, as area: the habitat within radius (source_strength), counted by how easily it is reached across the resistance surface; or, with a destination, the same between two distributions in both directions. Where dp_omni() and dp_flux() map where movement passes, this maps how connected each place is. Every cell gets a value, not only habitat, so it also shows how connected a site would be there.

A cell's targets are the cells of its connected component within radius and beyond its own site (see "Sites"), weighted by target strength \(t\). Three layers describe them:

accessible_area

The targets in reach, counted by how easily they are reached: \(\mathrm{target\_area}_i \, C_i / C^*\), where \(C_i\) is conductance and \(C^*\) is the conductance a site would have in continuous habitat (every cell a target, of resistance reference_resistance) at the same radius and site_radius. Targets as easy to reach as in continuous habitat count in full, and harder ones proportionally less; targets close to the site, or through resistance below the reference, can count for more. It responds to the amount of targets, their arrangement and the resistance surface together.

target_area

The targets in reach as area, each cell's area weighted by its target strength: \(\sum_{j \notin S_i} t_j a_j k(d_{ij})\), with \(S_i\) the cell's site, \(a_j\) the cell's area and \(k\) 1 within radius and 0 otherwise. For a 0-1 suitability it is the area of suitable habitat in reach; for strengths above 1 it is an area-equivalent, and can exceed the area in reach. It is exact, and ignores resistance.

conductance

The effective conductance from the site to its targets as a set: one over the effective resistance when one unit of current leaves the site and is withdrawn across its targets in proportion to their strength. Many targets in reach act like parallel paths and raise it. Its inverse is the injection of dp_flux() with the one site as the origin. It doesn't respond to how much target there is: thinning every target to a tenth of its strength leaves it unchanged, which is what accessible_area adds.

Areas are in square kilometres where the grid's coordinate reference system gives cell areas (on lon/lat grids, per row, on a sphere), and in cells otherwise; the "area_units" attribute says which. Cells without targets in reach (none within radius and beyond their site, in the same component) score 0 on all three layers. These include cells of pieces of the circuit not much wider than a site, such as small islands, whose site holds the whole piece.

With a destination, each cell is scored in both directions, with origin_ and destination_ prefixes on the layers. The origin_ layers take the cell as an origin, with the destination (destination) as its targets: how well could movement from here reach the destination? The destination_ layers take the cell as a destination, with the origin (source_strength) as its targets: how reachable is this place from the origin? For present and future habitat, the first asks which populations can track their habitat, the second which future habitat can be colonised. Effective resistance is symmetric, so the two differ only in their targets.

Sites

Each cell stands for a site: the cells within site_radius pixels of it (2 by default), across which the current is spread evenly. Targets are sites too, so conductances are between the sites around cells. A site is never its own target: a cell's targets are the habitat beyond its site, so radius must reach beyond the site.

Sites correct for the grid. On a grid, the effective resistance from a single cell grows only with the log of distance, so most of it is in the first few rings of links around the cell. A single cell's value is then dominated by its own contact resistance, the resistance of its own links in parallel, and maps the cell's own resistance more than its place in the landscape. A site a couple of cells in radius keeps that local term from dominating, as Circuitscape's focal regions do. Because the problem is the grid's, site_radius is in pixels whatever radius_units, and is not the dispersal scale: that is radius.

Values depend on the site, so compare runs at the same site. On grids of different resolution, the same number of pixels is a different site (between 2 km and 0.5 km grids, median accessible area shifted by about 10%, and more in core habitat); to compare resolutions, scale site_radius to keep the same ground distance.

With site_radius = 0, each site is its single cell, and its own resistance is part of its value: the reading for a single point of interest. With contact = TRUE, the result includes the contact layer, each cell's contact conductance (its own links in parallel, exact), an upper bound on the single-cell conductance.

The continuous-habitat reference

\(C^*\) is solved exactly, once per kernel, on a uniform grid wide enough that its edges don't matter, and is inversely proportional to reference_resistance: set that to the resistance of good habitat. On lon/lat grids with radius_units = "km", the kernel varies by row, and so does \(C^*\); rows within reach of the top or bottom of the grid use the nearest row whose kernel fits, so that there, as at other edges, the grid's edge lowers accessible area rather than the reference. With radius = Inf, continuous habitat has no finite reference, and the result has no accessible_area layer.

A larger radius raises target_area everywhere and accessible_area almost everywhere, but not at every cell: the current is withdrawn from the targets in fixed proportions, so where widening the radius adds mostly hard-to-reach targets, it lowers the conductance to all of them, and accessible area can fall.

Method

Each draw injects a random-sign dipole across every link of the circuit, scaled by the square root of the link's conductance, and solves the circuit once. For the solution \(y\), \((y_i - y_j)^2\) is then an unbiased estimate of the effective resistance between \(i\) and \(j\) for every pair at once, and the resistance to the targets comes from sums of \(y\) over each cell's targets, after averaging \(y\) over each site. Its mean over draws estimates the resistance without bias; conductance and accessible_area invert it, corrected for the bias of inverting a noisy estimate. target_area and all window sums use per-row running sums, at a cost linear in the radius.

Flow potential has no direct analogue here. With normalize, the same draws on the uniform circuit (conductance 1 on the same cells, with the same targets) give the conductance for geometry alone, and normalized_conductance divides by it: the conductance of a uniform landscape of the same shape that would give the same value, in the units of the input's conductance. A value of 0.5 means the cell is as connected as it would be if every cell had resistance 2. Below the landscape's typical conductance, the cell is isolated by its resistances; above, by geometry (distance, edges, few targets) more than by resistance. Unlike accessible_area, it compares each cell with its own geometry, so it doesn't respond to the amount of targets either.

Accuracy

Each draw's resistance estimate is a squared Gaussian-like quantity, so the relative standard error of conductance and accessible_area is about \(\sqrt{2 / \mathrm{n\_draws}}\) at any grid size: about 18% at the default 64 draws, and 10% at 200. Both circuits see the same draws, so on landscapes of modest contrast the noise of normalized_conductance largely cancels, but where resistance varies by orders of magnitude it doesn't. With se = TRUE, the result includes each estimated layer's per-cell standard error; the "relative_se" attribute gives each estimated layer's median relative standard error either way.

Reproducibility, performance and progress are as for dp_omni(): one factorization (two with normalize), then about n_draws solves, plus a small factorization and one solve per kernel for the reference.

See also

dp_omni(), dp_flux(), dp_circuit()

Examples

if (FALSE) { # circuitscaper::cs_julia_available(circuitscape = FALSE)
resistance <- terra::rast(system.file("extdata/resistance.tif",
                                      package = "circuitscaper"))
result <- dp_accessibility(resistance, radius = 15, seed = 1)
terra::plot(result)
attr(result, "area_units")
attr(result, "relative_se")

# Between two distributions, in both directions
origin <- terra::rast(system.file("extdata/source.tif", package = "circuitscaper"))
destination <- terra::rast(system.file("extdata/ground.tif", package = "circuitscaper"))
between <- dp_accessibility(resistance, radius = 45, source_strength = origin,
                            destination = destination, normalize = FALSE, seed = 1)
terra::plot(between)
DONTSHOW({JuliaConnectoR::stopJulia()})
}
